items.rationale: The model keeps no state between sessions; the message list is discarded at the end, so only information the program saved and reloaded reaches the next session. Choosing a shows the belief that window size governs cross-session memory; b shows the belief that the model learns from use.

Calls read 1,000, 1,500 and 2,000 tokens, total 4,500; equivalently 3 x 1,000 + 500 x 3 x 2 / 2 = 3,000 + 1,500. An answer of 3,000 forgets that each call also resends earlier additions; 2,000 counts only the last call.

Retrieval puts only the relevant chunks in the context, so far fewer tokens are resent on each of the 5 calls, and the answer is not buried in a long input. Loading everything because it fits shows the belief that the window limit is what matters.

items.answer: Models use long contexts less reliably: recall drops as tokens grow, and information in the middle is used worst.
accepted: recall decreases as the context gets longer
information in the middle of a long context is often missed
the model can miss relevant details buried in a long context
items.rationale: Context rot and the position effect (Liu et al.) mean a larger context can reduce accuracy, not just raise cost.

Clearing old tool results removes unneeded tokens, and a saved note is the only thing that survives across sessions. Relying on a summary can lose the detail, and keeping everything raises cost and context rot.
